## Core Overview

Lecture 06 focuses on measuring the efficiency of non-recursive algorithms through exact operation counting using a simplified Random Access Memory (RAM) model. The primary objective is to build machine-independent mathematical descriptions of work before applying asymptotic notation in subsequent lectures.

## Key Concepts & Formulas

- Simplified RAM Model: An idealized teaching abstraction that assumes sequential instruction execution, unit-cost simple primitive operations, constant-cost memory access (reading/writing), and ignores hardware details like CPU caches and compilers.
- Systematic 5-Step Analysis Recipe:
  1. Size: Define n precisely (e.g., number of array elements, characters, or matrix dimensions).
  2. Basic Op: Identify the repeated operation whose execution dominates the workload.
  3. Count: Determine how many times the basic operation executes.
  4. Cases: Evaluate whether input arrangements affect the workload.
  5. Formula: Express the total work as a function, such as C(n) or T(n).
- Case Analysis Categories:
  - Best Case: Minimum work among all valid inputs of size n (C_best(n) = 1 for linear search when target is at index 0).
  - Worst Case: Maximum work among all valid inputs of size n (C_worst(n) = n for linear search with an absent target).
  - Average Case: Expected work under a stated probability model (C_avg(n) = (n + 1) / 2 for successful linear search under uniform distribution).
- Mathematical Formulas for Loops:
  - Single loops iterating n times yield linear counts: C(n) = n.
  - Nested loops where the inner loop depends on the outer loop index sum to arithmetic series: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1) / 2.

## Exam Takeaways

- Always define n explicitly before writing any formula like T(n) or C(n).
- State your probability model clearly when calculating average case behavior; an average case without assumptions is meaningless.
- Distinguish between best-case arrangement and small input size: an algorithm can receive a large input and still hit the best case due to favorable arrangement (e.g., target found at the first position).
- Avoid common pitfalls: never count different operations interchangeably without stating it, and always derive exact counts before jumping to Big-O notation.
